finding.claim: The /settings/email POST route uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid=None. This is a missing authentication check on a state-changing account operation. Its sibling /settings/password uses login_required.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, which changes an account email with uid None

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid') (None when anonymous) and calls the handler without aborting
set_email(g.uid, ...) is invoked with no auth enforced

finding.guards_checked: login_required is on /settings/password (routes.py:42) but not on this route. No other check (ownership, CSRF, uid None check) exists in the handler. /feed also uses login_optional, but it is read-only with an empty result, so it is safe.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 only sets g.uid and never aborts; no uid None check in handler)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies login_optional, which at routes.py:22-23 sets g.uid=None for anonymous callers and still runs the handler, so routes.py:37 calls set_email(None, ...) with no auth check, unlike login_required at routes.py:11-12 which aborts 401. Caveat: set_email at routes.py:48-49 is a stub, so the real impact depends on its implementation.
